title: Logit Distance Bounds Representational Similarity
claim: Closeness under a logit-based distance guarantees similar linear representations, whereas closeness under KL does not, as shown by preserved versus lost concept structure.
layout: 3 panels, center-diagram flanked by left/right embedding plots, dotted connectors
description: Three-part figure. The center shows two stacked ellipses. The upper ellipse is the quotient space Θ/∼_L with identifiability classes [(f,g)], [(f',g')] and [(f*,g*)]. The lower ellipse is the distribution space P_Θ with points p_{f,g}, p_{f',g'} and p_{f*,g*}. A small blue region marks the d_logit ≤ ε ball and a larger pink region marks the d_KL ≤ ε ball. Dotted arrows link points between the two ellipses. A blue arrow and a pink arrow show the bounds. Dotted lines run from the center points to the side panels. The left panel is an LDA scatter plot of embeddings for the logit-trained student. It shows clean colored clusters over colored background regions, with bird photos around the edges. The right panel is the same plot for the KL-trained student. It shows a mixed, overlapping blob of points. A color legend of six bird attributes runs along the bottom.
caption: In the center: The intuition of bounding representational similarity using distributional distance. $\calP_\Theta$ is the set of probability distributions parametrized by models in $\Theta$ (Eq. [ref]) which satisfy [ref]. These distributions are one-to-one with identifiability classes $[(\vf, \vg)] $ in the quotient space $\Theta / \sim_L$ [ref]. The colored areas in $\calP_\Theta$ contain the distributions which are $\epsilon$-close to a reference $p_{\vf, \vg}$, as measured by $d_\mathrm{logit}$ ([ref], blue area) or by $d_\mathrm{KL}$ (Eq. [ref], pink area). Our [ref] lower-bounds representational similarity (in terms of $m_{\mathrm{CCA}}$, blue arrow) using the logit distance $d_{\mathrm{logit}}$; similarly, [ref] upper-bounds dissimilarity in terms of our $d_{\mathrm{rep}}$ ([ref]). In [ref] (pink arrow) we prove that $d_\mathrm{KL}$ yields weak bounds on $d_{\mathrm{logit}}$. We illustrate this with representations of two student models distilled from a teacher on the \SUB dataset [ref], see [ref] for details. On the left, a student model trained to minimize a variant of $d_\mathrm{logit}$ ([ref]) to the teacher distribution $p_{\vf, \vg}$ preserves linearly encoded concepts ([ref]): for $6$ attributes, we visualize their linear separability in the embeddings by projecting them to two dimensions through LDA [ref]. Distinct concept attributes can be well separated linearly in this $2$d subspace. On the right, for a model trained to minimize $d_\mathrm{KL}$ the LDA reduction shows that different concept attributes are not linearly separable, as reflected by the extremely low accuracy in [ref].
abstract: For a broad family of discriminative models that includes autoregressive language models, identifiability results imply that if two models induce the same conditional distributions, then their internal representations are equal up to an invertible linear transformation. We ask whether an analogous conclusion holds approximately when the distributions are close instead of equal. Building on the observation of Nielsen et al. (2025) that closeness in KL divergence need not imply high linear representational similarity, we study a distributional distance based on logit differences and show that closeness in this distance does yield linear similarity guarantees. Specifically, we define a representational dissimilarity measure based on the models' identifiability class and prove that it is bounded by the logit distance. We further show that, when model probabilities are bounded away from zero, KL divergence upper-bounds logit distance; yet the resulting bound fails to provide nontrivial control in practice. As a consequence, KL-based distillation can match a teacher's predictions while failing to preserve linear representational properties, such as linear-probe recoverability of human-interpretable concepts. In distillation experiments on synthetic and image datasets, logit-distance distillation yields students with higher linear representational similarity and better preservation of the teacher's linearly recoverable concepts.
